841.quote_or_event: “All men who are ignorant of the Truth are subject to pain; in the endless Samsâra they suffer in many ways.”
841.explanation: The lecture on the false ascetic opens by making ignorance of the truth the root of every kind of suffering across endless rebirth, and goes on to urge the wise to search for the truth themselves.
841.tie_back: Valluvar calls lack of understanding the real poverty among all poverties, and Mahavira's sermon likewise treats ignorance, not any lack of goods, as the want that causes all other suffering.
841.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
841._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (only the italic markup in 'Samsâra' is normalised). It shares the Kural's ranking of ignorance as the deepest misfortune but does not explicitly compare it with poverty of wealth.

842.quote_or_event: The Tattvārtha Sūtra teaches that the merit of a gift is not fixed. It varies with four things: the manner of giving, the thing given, the giver, and the worthiness of the recipient (pātra).
842.explanation: In Jain teaching on charity (dāna), a gift's fruit depends partly on who receives it, which is why a worthy recipient such as a restrained monk adds to the merit of the offering.
842.tie_back: The Kural ironically credits a fool's glad gift to the recipient's own merit, and Jain dāna theory likewise counts the recipient's worthiness as one of the things that decide what a gift is worth.
842.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39 (Digambara numbering; 7.34 in the Śvetāmbara recension), Umāsvāti; cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain, wisdomlib.org
842._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutra whose numbering I confirmed only through a search snippet this session, not the full page. It matches the idea that the recipient shapes the gift but has none of the Kural's irony about the fool, so it is a next-best match.

843.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
843.explanation: In the commentarial story, the burglar is crushed by the very wall he dug through, an image of how each soul's own deeds (karma) come back on it.
843.tie_back: The Kural says fools hurt themselves more than any enemy could, and the Jain burglar dies in the hole he cut himself, so the ruin is his own work and no enemy's.
843.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
843._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Self-inflicted ruin is a strong fit, but the verse does not explicitly compare it with harm done by enemies.

844.quote_or_event: “Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
844.explanation: Mahavira mocks people who rely on fine words and doctrine without right conduct, and names as the mark of the fool his belief that he is wise.
844.tie_back: Valluvar defines folly as the conceit that says 'we are wise', and the Uttarādhyayana gives the same definition: the fool sinks while he believes himself wise.
844.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
844._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The second sentence is almost one to one with the Kural's definition of folly as conceit of wisdom.

845.quote_or_event: In its chapter on purity of speech, the Daśavaikālika Sūtra tells the monk that where there is doubt about a matter, he must not declare 'it is just so'. He may speak with certainty only about what he truly knows.
845.explanation: Jain monastic rules on speech forbid asserting as certain anything one does not know, because false certainty breaks the vow of truthfulness (satya).
845.tie_back: The Kural warns that pretending to know what one never learned makes people doubt even one's real knowledge, and the Jain rule removes the cause by forbidding any confident claim beyond what one knows.
845.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra ch. 7 (Vākyaśuddhi, 'purity of speech'), Prakrit 'jattha saṃkā bhave taṃ tu, evameyaṃ ti no vae'
845._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the Prakrit line was confirmed only through a search snippet and I could not pin the verse number or an English translation online, so it is not quoted. It shares the theme of not claiming unearned knowledge but leaves out the Kural's point that genuine knowledge then loses credit.

846.quote_or_event: Kundakunda's Liṅga-pāhuḍa teaches that what makes a true mendicant is the inner disposition (bhāva-liṅga), and that the outward form (dravya-liṅga), even the Digambara monk's total nudity, does not make anyone a true monk.
846.explanation: For the Digambara master, how the body is presented, clothed or naked, is worthless unless the inner faults of passion are removed.
846.tie_back: Valluvar calls it folly to cover the body carefully while leaving one's faults exposed, and Kundakunda, from the other side, says that even giving up all clothing achieves nothing while those inner faults remain.
846.source: Kundakunda, Liṅga-pāhuḍa (with Bhāva-pāhuḍa), as summarised by Jainpedia, 'Kundakunda'
846._accuracy_note: Paraphrase based on a secondary summary (Jainpedia), not a primary translation; no verse number given. The principle that outward bodily form counts for nothing without inner purity fits well, though the Jain case is about nudity rather than covering the body.

847.quote_or_event: “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
847.explanation: The lecture on discipline contrasts the wise pupil who values a teacher's correction with the fool who rejects the very counsel that would help him.
847.tie_back: On the reading of the Kural in which the fool lets precious counsel slip and so harms himself, the Uttarādhyayana gives the same picture: the fool hates the instruction that would have made him patient and pure.
847.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
847._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It fits the 'neglected good advice' reading of arumarai but not the traditional 'failing to keep a secret' reading.

848.quote_or_event: “Whether he know the pith of the Law by intuition or through instruction, a houseless (monk) should exert himself and abstain from sins.”
848.explanation: Jain teaching recognises two routes to right understanding, one's own insight and being taught by others, and expects right effort to follow from either.
848.tie_back: Valluvar condemns the person who neither acts when told nor works things out himself, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga names exactly those two routes, intuition and instruction, as the ways the earnest seeker comes to know the Law.
848.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
848._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It has the Kural's two routes (being told and knowing for oneself) but states the positive ideal rather than condemning someone who has neither, and it lacks the 'lifelong disease' image.

849.quote_or_event: “Now this driver (viz. Garga), who had to deal with bad bullocks, thought: 'What have I to do with bad pupils? I am disheartened. 'As are bad pupils, so are bad bullocks; I shall leave these lazy donkeys, and shall practise severe austerities.'”
849.explanation: The learned elder Garga, worn out by pupils who argue and will not be convinced by reasons, finally gives up teaching them and turns to his own austerities.
849.tie_back: The Kural warns that whoever tries to show the truth to a fool ends up looking foolish himself, and Garga's story shows the same trap: the teacher tires himself out and has to walk away.
849.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 27.15–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
849._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com, including his nested quotation marks. It matches the futility of instructing the obstinate but not the Kural's twist that the instructor himself is taken for a fool.

850.quote_or_event: “A monk should not think: 'There is, indeed, no life to come, nor an exalted state to be acquired by penances; in short, I have been deceived.'”
850.explanation: Among the twenty-two troubles a monk must overcome, the last is the temptation to deny what the Jinas taught: the next life, the fruit of austerity, and the Jinas themselves.
850.tie_back: The Kural's fool flatly denies what the wise affirm, such as the other world and the fruit of deeds, and the Uttarādhyayana lists exactly this denial as a failing of right faith to be overcome.
850.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.44 (cf. 2.45) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
850._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The content of the denial matches the traditional gloss closely, but the Jain verse is an inner warning to monks and says nothing of the society shunning the denier as a demon.
